questions.question:
For any two languages L1 and L2 such that L1 is context-free and L2 is recursively enumerable but not recursive, which of the following is/are necessarily true?
I. [latex]\bar{L_{1}}[/latex] (complement of L1) is recursive
II. [latex] \bar{L_{2}}[/latex] (complement of L2) is recursive
III. [latex]\bar{L_{1}}[/latex] is context-free
IV. [latex]\bar{L_{1}} \cup L_{2}[/latex] is recursively enumerable
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- I: CFLs are decidable, and recursive languages are closed under complement [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True
- II: if [latex]\bar L_2[/latex] were recursive, L2 would be recursive [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False
- III: CFLs are not closed under complement [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not necessarily
- IV: [latex]\bar L_1[/latex] is recursive (so RE), and RE is closed under union [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True

Answer: I and IV only

questions.question: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?

options.C: Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.

questions.explanation:
A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA.

Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA.

"Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable.

Answer: Any regular language.

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Consider the context-free grammars over the alphabet {a,b,c} given below. S and T are non-terminals

[latex]G_{1}:S\rightarrow aSb|T, T\rightarrow cT|\epsilon[/latex] [latex]G_{2}:S\rightarrow bSa|T,T\rightarrow cT|\epsilon[/latex]

The language [latex]L(G_{1})\cap L(G_{2})[/latex] is
questions.explanation:
[latex]L(G_1)=\{a^nc^mb^n\}[/latex] and [latex]L(G_2)=\{b^nc^ma^n\}[/latex]. A common string must have n = 0 in both (otherwise one starts with a and the other with b), so the intersection is [latex]c^*[/latex]: infinite but regular.

Answer: Not finite but regular

questions.question:
Consider the alphabet [latex]\Sigma[/latex]={0, 1}, the null/empty string [latex]\lambda[/latex] and the sets of strings [latex]X_{0}, X_{1}, \; and \; X_{2}[/latex] generated by the corresponding non-terminals of a regular grammar. [latex]X_{0}, X_{1}, \; and \; X_{2}[/latex] are related as follows.
[latex]X_{0}=1X_{1}[/latex]
[latex]X_{1},=0X_{1}+1 X_{2}[/latex]
[latex]X_{2}=0X_{1}+ \{\lambda\}[/latex]
Which one of the following choices precisely represents the strings in [latex]X_{0}[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Substitute [latex]X_2[/latex] into [latex]X_1[/latex]:
[latex]X_1=0X_1+1(0X_1+\lambda)=(0+10)X_1+1[/latex]

By Arden's rule [latex]X_1=(0+10)^*1[/latex], so [latex]X_0=1(0+10)^*1[/latex].

Answer: 1(0 + 10)*1

questions.question:
Definition of a language L with alphabet {a} is given as following L={[latex]a^{nk}[/latex] |k > 0, and n is a positive integer constant}
What is the minimum number of states needed in a DFA to recognize L?
questions.explanation:
L = {[latex]a^n, a^{2n}, a^{3n}, \dots[/latex]} (length a positive multiple of n).

States [latex]q_0,\dots,q_n[/latex]: count up to n, accept at [latex]q_n[/latex], then [latex]q_n[/latex] loops back through [latex]q_1..q_n[/latex]. The empty string must be rejected, so [latex]q_0[/latex] is separate.

That is n + 1 states.

Answer: n + 1

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:
I. If all states of an NFA are accepting states then the language accepted by the NFA is [latex]\sum ^{*}[/latex] .

questions.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the set of terminals is [latex]\{a,b,c,d,f\}[/latex].

[latex]\begin{array}{lll} S & \rightarrow & d \: a \: T \mid R \: f \\ T & \rightarrow & a \: S \: \mid \: b \: a \: T \: \mid \epsilon \\ R & \rightarrow & c \: a \: T \: R \: \mid \epsilon \end{array}[/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

Which one of the following choices represents the correct combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table ("blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty)?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]FIRST(Rf)=\{c,f\}[/latex] (R can be [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (1) [S, c] and (2) [S, f] are both [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex].
- [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes in FOLLOW(T). T is followed by R in [latex]R\rightarrow caTR[/latex] (gives c, and FOLLOW(R) = {f}), and FOLLOW(T) includes FOLLOW(S) = {$}. So FOLLOW(T) = {c, f, $}.
- (3) [T, c] = [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] and (4) [T, $] = [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].

Answer: A

questions.question:
Let [latex]\Sigma = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}[/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^*[/latex], let [latex]\text{prod}(x)[/latex] be the product of symbols in [latex]x[/latex] modulo 7. We take [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon) = 1[/latex], where [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is the null string.

For example, [latex]\text{prod}(124) = (1 \times 2 \times 4) \mod 7 = 1[/latex].

Define [latex] L = \{x \in \Sigma^* \mid \text{prod}(x) = 2\}. [/latex]

The number of states in a minimum state DFA for [latex]L[/latex] is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Since the alphabet [latex]\{1,2,3,4\}[/latex] contains no multiple of [latex]7[/latex] and no [latex]0[/latex], the running product modulo [latex]7[/latex] can never become [latex]0[/latex] — it always stays within the [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues [latex]\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}[/latex].

A minimal DFA for this language just needs one state per possible running-product value (tracking "current product mod 7 so far," starting at the state for [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon)=1[/latex]), with the state representing residue [latex]2[/latex] being the unique accepting state. Since multiplying by [latex]1,2,3,4[/latex] can move between any pair of these [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues in different ways, all [latex]6[/latex] states are reachable and pairwise distinguishable (no two can be merged without changing the language).

Answer: 6

questions.question:
Consider the languages
[latex]L1=\{0^{i}1^{j}\;| \; i\neq j\}[/latex].
[latex]L2=\{0^{i}1^{j}\;| \; i=j\}[/latex].
[latex]L3=\{0^{i}1^{j}\;| \; i=2j+1\}[/latex].
[latex]L4=\{0^{i}1^{j}\;| \; i \neq 2j\}[/latex]
Which one of the following statements is true?

options.B: Only L2 and L3 are context free
options.C: Only L1 and L3 are context free

questions.explanation:
Each needs only one counter comparison, which one stack can do:
- L1: [latex]0^i1^j[/latex], i [latex]\ne[/latex] j
- L2: [latex]0^i1^i[/latex]
- L3: push 2 per 1 (check i = 2j + 1)
- L4: i [latex]\ne[/latex] 2j

All are context-free.

Answer: All are context free

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about regular languages:

S1: Every infinite regular language contains an undecidable language as a subset.
S2: Every finite language is regular.

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.C: Both S1 and S2 are true
options.D: Neither S1 nor S2 is true

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: an infinite language has uncountably many subsets, but only countably many are decidable. So some subset is undecidable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- S2: a finite language is a finite union of single strings [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

questions.question: Let [latex] G=(V, \Sigma, S, P) [/latex] be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with [latex] \Sigma=\{a, b, c\} [/latex] and [latex] V [/latex] containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol [latex] S [/latex]. The string [latex] w=a^{30} b^{30} c^{30} [/latex] is derivable from [latex] S [/latex]. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation [latex] S \rightarrow^* w [/latex] is _____
questions.explanation:
CNF rules are [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] or [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex].

- Each [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] increases the number of symbols by 1. To grow from 1 symbol (S) to [latex]n[/latex] symbols needs [latex]n-1[/latex] such steps.
- Each of the [latex]n[/latex] variables is then turned into a terminal by [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex]: [latex]n[/latex] steps.

Total [latex]=2n-1[/latex]. Here [latex]n=|w|=90[/latex]: [latex]2(90)-1=179[/latex].

Answer: 179
